units.title: Stories of Old
units.overview: This unit is all about traditional tales: stories that people have told and retold for hundreds of years. You will read fables, where animals teach us a lesson, and folktales, where ordinary people meet tricky problems. By the end, you will write a traditional tale of your own.
objectives: Explain the structure of a fable (opening, climax and resolution) and what a moral is.
Compare fables and folktales and spot their similarities and differences.
Write simple and complex sentences, and use commas to separate clauses.
Work out the meaning of unknown words from context using the IDEAS strategy.
Spell words with the letter strings ‘ie’ and ‘ou’, and understand common idioms.
Read a story aloud with expression, and plan, write and improve your own fable or folktale.

texts.title: The Tales of Anansi
texts.kind: Fables from West Africa and the Caribbean
texts.summary: Anansi is a clever but greedy spider from West African stories. In the first tale, he wants to taste everyone’s cooking, so he ties strands of web from his legs to his friends’ cooking pots. When all the food is ready at the same moment, his legs are pulled in every direction, which explains why spiders have long, thin legs. In the other tales, Anansi tries to keep all the world’s wisdom for himself in a gourd, but his own son shows him a better idea, and the wisdom ends up being shared with everyone.

texts.title: The Man Who Never Lied
texts.summary: Madan is famous because he never tells a lie. The king tries to trick him into telling one, but Madan only ever reports exactly what he has seen. In the end, it is the king who looks foolish, and Madan’s honesty is proved.

texts.title: The Fisherman and His Wife
texts.summary: A poor fisherman catches a magic talking fish and lets it go. His wife makes him ask the fish for one wish after another, each one bigger than the last. Because she is never satisfied, she loses everything she was given. The story is about greed and its consequences.

vocab.meaning: A short story, usually with animal characters, that teaches a lesson.
vocab.example: ‘The Tortoise and the Hare’ is a famous fable.

vocab.meaning: The lesson about life that a story teaches.
vocab.example: The moral of the story is ‘Do not be greedy’.

vocab.meaning: A traditional story, usually about people, passed down by word of mouth for many years.
vocab.example: Grandma told us a folktale from her village.

vocab.meaning: The most exciting part of a story, when the problem is at its biggest.
vocab.example: At the climax, Anansi’s legs were pulled in eight directions.

vocab.meaning: The end of a story, when the problem is sorted out.
vocab.example: In the resolution, everyone shared the wisdom.

vocab.meaning: Clever at getting what you want, often by tricking others.
vocab.example: The cunning fox fooled the crow.

vocab.meaning: Wanting much more of something than you need.
vocab.example: The greedy boy took all the sweets.

vocab.meaning: Always telling the truth.
vocab.example: Madan was honest, even when the king tried to trick him.

vocab.meaning: A sentence with a main clause and at least one dependent clause.
vocab.example: When the bell rang, the children lined up quietly.

vocab.meaning: A group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words.
vocab.example: ‘The cherry on the top’ means something that makes a good thing even better.

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Simple and complex sentences

sb.title: Reading Part 1: The Man Who Never Lied

sb.title: Reading Part 2: The Fisherman and His Wife and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: Track each wish the wife makes. How does the fish’s reply change each time?

sb.title: Language Focus – Vocabulary: Idioms
sb.tip: An idiom does not mean exactly what its words say. Think about the whole meaning, not the separate words.

sb.title: Speaking: Reading aloud
sb.tip: Practise at home. Read slowly and clearly, pause at commas and full stops, and change your voice for different characters.

sb.title: Writing: Your own fable or folktale
sb.tip: Plan first. Choose your characters, setting and problem, and decide how the problem will be solved. If you are writing a fable, add a moral.

sb.title: Unit Self-reflection
sb.tip: Be honest about what you found easy and what you need to practise more.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a fable?
cards.back: Opening (characters and setting), climax (the problem at its biggest) and resolution (the problem is solved and the moral is given).

cards.front: How is a folktale different from a fable?
cards.back: Folktales are mostly about people and do not always have a moral. Fables are mostly about animals and always teach a lesson.

cards.front: What does the IDEAS strategy stand for?
cards.back: Infer, Define, Example, Antonym and Synonym. These are five ways to use context to work out a new word.

cards.front: Why does Anansi end up with long, thin legs?
cards.back: He tied a strand of web to each friend’s pot, and all the food was ready at once, so his legs were pulled in every direction.

cards.front: What is the lesson of ‘The Fisherman and His Wife’?
cards.back: Greed has consequences. The wife kept wanting more and lost everything.

cards.front: How do you spot a complex sentence?
cards.back: It has a main clause plus a dependent clause, often starting with a word like ‘when’, ‘because’, ‘as’ or ‘if’.

practice.q: Which of these is a feature of a fable?
options: It always has a happy ending
practice.explain: Fables teach a moral, which is a lesson about life.

practice.q: Which part of a story is the climax?
options: The part where the characters are introduced
The most exciting part, when the problem is biggest
practice.explain: The climax is the turning point, when the problem reaches its most important moment.

practice.q: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: When the beans were ready, the rabbit tugged the web.
practice.explain: It has a main clause (‘the rabbit tugged the web’) and a dependent clause (‘When the beans were ready’).

practice.q: Where should the commas go? ‘My cousin who lives in Doha loves folktales.’
options: My cousin, who lives in Doha, loves folktales.
My, cousin who lives in Doha loves folktales.
My cousin who lives, in Doha loves, folktales.
practice.explain: The commas go around the extra information, ‘who lives in Doha’.

practice.q: Which word has the ‘ie’ letter string making an ‘ee’ sound?
practice.explain: In ‘field’, ‘ie’ sounds like ‘ee’. In the other words, it sounds like ‘igh’.

practice.q: What does the idiom ‘over the moon’ mean?
practice.explain: An idiom has a meaning that is different from its words. ‘Over the moon’ means delighted.

practice.q: In the IDEAS strategy, what does the ‘A’ stand for?
practice.explain: An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning, and it can help you work out a new word.

practice.q: Folktales are usually…
options: stories passed down by word of mouth for many generations
practice.explain: Folktales are traditional stories that people have told and retold for a very long time.

units.title: True Stories About Real People
units.overview: In this unit you will read biographies: true stories about the lives of real people. You will meet a famous showman and three remarkable women from history, and you will learn how biographers find out about people’s lives. At the end, you will research and write a short biography of your own.
objectives: Describe the structure and features of a biography, from the introduction to the person’s legacy.
Use modal verbs such as ‘can’, ‘might’, ‘must’ and ‘should’ correctly.
Use prefixes and suffixes to make new words and opposites.
Split long words into syllables and spot silent letters.
Use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, and use a thesaurus.
Research, plan and write a short biography using different sources of information.

texts.title: P.T. Barnum and the Greatest Show on Earth
texts.summary: Phineas Taylor Barnum (1810–1891) was an American showman. He started a museum full of unusual attractions in New York and later built an enormous travelling circus, known as ‘The Greatest Show on Earth’, which moved from town to town by train. One of his most famous attractions was Jumbo, a giant elephant. Barnum even managed to read his own obituary in a newspaper before he died!

texts.title: Women Who Mattered
texts.summary: Two short biographies of brave and determined women. Bibi Rajindar Kaur, from Patiala in northern India, led an army to help her family and helped to arrange peace talks. Wang Zhenyi, from China, taught herself astronomy and mathematics at a time when girls could not go to school, and explained eclipses using experiments she set up at home.

texts.title: A Woman of Vision
texts.summary: This biography tells the story of Wangari Maathai from Kenya. She saw that forests were being cut down and the land was drying out, so she encouraged women to plant trees, which helped the environment and gave them an income. She became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

vocab.meaning: The true story of a person’s life, written by someone else.
vocab.example: I read a biography of a famous scientist.

vocab.meaning: Something important that a person leaves behind for the world after they die.
vocab.example: Her legacy is the millions of trees that she helped to plant.

vocab.meaning: Something good and difficult that a person has done.
vocab.example: Winning the prize was her greatest achievement.

vocab.meaning: A piece of writing about someone’s life, published after they die.
vocab.example: The newspaper printed an obituary of the famous showman.

vocab.meaning: A place or thing that people go to see because it is interesting or fun.
vocab.example: The elephant was the circus’s biggest attraction.

vocab.meaning: The study of the stars, planets and space.
vocab.example: Wang Zhenyi loved astronomy.

vocab.meaning: Continuing to try hard, even when something is difficult.
vocab.example: With perseverance, she learnt to read difficult books.

vocab.meaning: A helping verb, such as ‘can’, ‘might’, ‘must’ or ‘should’, that shows how possible or necessary something is.
vocab.example: You should read every day.

vocab.meaning: A book or website that lists words with similar meanings (synonyms).
vocab.example: I used a thesaurus to find another word for ‘big’.

vocab.meaning: The form of an adjective or adverb that shows the most or the least, for example ‘tallest’ or ‘most careful’.
vocab.example: Jumbo was the biggest elephant in the circus.

sb.title: Be Curious
sb.tip: Talk about where you could find out about a real person’s life, such as books, encyclopaedias and websites.

sb.title: Getting Started
sb.tip: Think of a famous person you admire. What would you want to know about their life?

sb.title: Let’s Learn: Structure and features of a biography
sb.tip: A biography is usually in the past tense and the third person (‘he’, ‘she’, ‘they’). It often has subheadings such as early life, achievements and legacy.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: P.T. Barnum and the Greatest Show on Earth

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Modal verbs
sb.tip: Some modal verbs show that something is certain (‘must’, ‘will’) and others show that it is only possible (‘might’, ‘could’).

sb.title: Reading Part 2: P.T. Barnum and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: Check each feature of a biography against the text. Can you find the dates, the past tense and the legacy?

sb.title: Language Focus – Vocabulary: Using prefixes, suffixes and root words
sb.tip: Prefixes such as ‘un-’, ‘im-’, ‘in-’ and ‘dis-’ can make opposites. The suffix ‘-less’ means ‘without’.

sb.title: Word Structure: Polysyllabic words
sb.tip: Clap the syllables. Each syllable has one vowel sound. Listen for silent letters, as in ‘handkerchief’.

sb.title: Writing: A plan for a biography
sb.tip: Choose your subject now. You will research and finish your biography in Part B.

sb.title: Getting Started and Let’s Learn: Sources of information
sb.tip: Biographers use family trees, maps, timelines, interviews and letters. Each one tells you something different.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: Women Who Mattered
sb.tip: For each woman, note the challenges she faced and what she achieved.

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs
sb.tip: Use comparatives to compare two things (‘smaller’, ‘more carefully’) and superlatives for three or more (‘smallest’, ‘most carefully’).

sb.title: Reading Part 2: A Woman of Vision and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: Find the reasons why Wangari Maathai thought trees were so important.

sb.title: Language Focus – Vocabulary: Using a thesaurus
sb.tip: A thesaurus gives you choices. Pick the synonym that fits the meaning of your sentence best.

sb.title: Speaking: Ask and answer questions
sb.tip: Prepare open questions that start with ‘how’, ‘why’ or ‘what’, and listen carefully to the answers.

sb.title: Writing: A short biography
sb.tip: Write an introduction that sums up why your person is important, then follow the order of their life.

sb.title: Unit Self-reflection
sb.tip: Which biography did you find most interesting, and why?

wb.tip: Use the past tense and the third person throughout.

cards.front: What are the usual parts of a biography?
cards.back: Introduction, early life, later life, achievements and legacy.

cards.front: Which tense and viewpoint does a biography use?
cards.back: The past tense and the third person (‘he’, ‘she’, ‘they’).

cards.front: What was ‘The Greatest Show on Earth’?
cards.back: P.T. Barnum’s enormous travelling circus, which moved from town to town by train.

cards.front: Why is Wangari Maathai remembered?
cards.back: She encouraged people to plant trees to protect the environment, and she was the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

cards.front: Name four sources of information a biographer might use.
cards.back: For example, family trees, maps, timelines, interviews and letters.

cards.front: When do you use ‘more’ and ‘most’ instead of ‘-er’ and ‘-est’?
cards.back: With most longer words, for example ‘more powerful’ and ‘most diligent’.

practice.q: A biography is…

practice.q: Which tense are most biographies written in?

practice.q: What is a person’s ‘legacy’?

units.title: Poets and Poetry
units.overview: This unit is about poems and the people who write them. You will read funny poems by an English poet and thoughtful nature poems by an American poet, then enjoy two poems that tell stories. You will use similes, metaphors and personification to write poems of your own.
objectives: Explain the difference between structured verse and free verse.
Identify rhyme, rhythm, repetition and stanzas in poems.
Recognise and use similes, metaphors and personification.
Use degrees of comparison correctly, for example ‘sad’, ‘sadder’ and ‘saddest’.
Spell words with the ‘sh’ sound written as ‘ti’, ‘ci’ and ‘ssi’.
Use synonyms and antonyms, and write a free verse poem.

texts.title: Poems by a Famous English Poet – Lewis Carroll
texts.summary: Lewis Carroll was an English writer who loved to entertain children with nonsense and humour. In ‘The Crocodile’, a crocodile seems to grin in a friendly way, but he is really welcoming little fishes into his jaws. ‘The Walrus and the Carpenter’ is a funny, rhyming poem about two odd characters walking along a beach.

texts.title: Poems by a Famous American Poet – Emily Dickinson
texts.summary: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) lived a quiet life in America and wrote many poems about nature. In ‘The Bee Is Not Afraid of Me’, nature treats the poet as a friend. ‘Autumn’ describes the changing season, and ‘The Butterfly’s Day’ is written in free verse, with short lines and dashes.

texts.title: Stone Soup
texts.kind: European folktale retold as a narrative poem
texts.summary: A hungry traveller arrives in a village with a big pot and claims he can make soup from a stone. One by one, the curious villagers add vegetables and other ingredients, until there is a delicious soup that everyone shares. The stone was never magic: it was the sharing that made the soup.

texts.title: The Spider and the Fly
texts.kind: Traditional narrative poem by Mary Howitt
texts.summary: A cunning spider invites a fly into his parlour. At first the fly refuses, but the spider keeps flattering her, and in the end she forgets her fear and flies in, with a sad result. The lesson is to beware of people who flatter you because they want something.

vocab.meaning: A group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in a story.
vocab.example: The poem has four stanzas.

vocab.meaning: Poetry that does not follow a fixed pattern of rhyme or rhythm.
vocab.example: “The Butterfly’s Day” is written in free verse.

vocab.meaning: The pattern of beats in a line of poetry.
vocab.example: Clap the rhythm as you read the poem aloud.

vocab.meaning: A comparison that uses ‘like’ or ‘as’.
vocab.example: She danced like a butterfly.

vocab.meaning: A comparison that says something is something else.
vocab.example: My little brother is my alarm clock.

vocab.meaning: Giving human actions or feelings to something that is not human.
vocab.example: The wind whispered through the trees.

vocab.meaning: A poem that tells a story, with characters and a plot.
vocab.example: “Stone Soup” is a narrative poem.

vocab.meaning: To praise someone too much, often to get something from them.
vocab.example: The spider flattered the fly to trick her.

vocab.meaning: A word with the same or a similar meaning as another word.
vocab.example: ‘Large’ is a synonym of ‘big’.

vocab.meaning: A word with the opposite meaning to another word.
vocab.example: ‘Polite’ is an antonym of ‘rude’.

sb.title: Be Curious and Getting Started
sb.tip: Talk about how poets and painters are alike. Both create things for other people to enjoy.

sb.title: Let’s Learn: Structured and free verse poems
sb.tip: Structured verse has a pattern of rhyme and rhythm. Free verse is more flexible and sounds more like natural speech.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: Poems by a Famous English Poet – Lewis Carroll
sb.tip: Read the poems aloud. Find the rhyming words and count the beats in each line.

units.title: The Workings of Machines
units.overview: How does a radio turn invisible waves into music and voices? In this unit you will read explanation texts that answer questions like this. You will learn how writers use headings, diagrams and flowcharts to make tricky ideas clear, and you will write your own explanation of how a machine works.
objectives: Identify the features of explanation texts, such as headings, subheadings, diagrams and the present simple tense.
Use infographics, keys, flowcharts and labelled diagrams to understand information.
Use countable and uncountable nouns with the right quantifiers, for example ‘fewer’ and ‘less’.
Find words quickly in alphabetical lists, such as dictionaries and glossaries.
Tell the difference between homophones, homographs and homonyms.
Reorder clauses in multi-clause sentences, and use specialised vocabulary in your own explanation.

texts.title: What Makes a Radio Work?
texts.summary: This explanation text tells you about electromagnetic waves, which travel through space, and how they are different from sound waves. It explains frequency (visible light has a higher frequency than radio waves) and shows how devices such as a remote-controlled car use an antenna to receive signals.

texts.title: How Does a Radio Work?
texts.summary: This text follows a message from start to finish. A transmitter turns sound waves into radio waves and sends them out. A receiver with an aerial picks them up, turns them back into sound and makes the sound louder, so that we can hear it. It also explains the two main kinds of radio broadcasting, AM and FM, using a flowchart and labelled pictures.

vocab.meaning: A non-fiction text that explains how or why something works or happens.
vocab.example: The explanation text showed how a radio works.

vocab.meaning: A device that sends out signals, such as radio waves.
vocab.example: The radio station’s transmitter sends out the signal.

vocab.meaning: A device that picks up signals and changes them into something we can use.
vocab.example: Your radio is a receiver.

vocab.meaning: A metal rod or wire that sends or receives radio waves (also called an aerial).
vocab.example: The car’s antenna picked up the signal.

vocab.meaning: How many times something happens, or how many waves pass a point, in a certain amount of time.
vocab.example: Visible light has a higher frequency than radio waves.

vocab.meaning: To make a sound louder.
vocab.example: The speaker amplifies the music.

vocab.meaning: A picture, chart or diagram that shows information clearly.
vocab.example: The flowchart is an infographic.

vocab.meaning: A word that tells you how much or how many, such as ‘some’, ‘few’, ‘little’ or ‘enough’.
vocab.example: There was less snow and fewer people this year.

vocab.meaning: A word that sounds the same as another word but has a different spelling and meaning.
vocab.example: ‘Right’ and ‘write’ are homophones.

vocab.meaning: An alphabetical list of special words and their meanings, usually at the back of a book.
vocab.example: I checked ‘frequency’ in the glossary.

units.title: Dangerous Creatures
units.overview: Snakes, jellyfish and cone snails all belong to ‘The Venom Club’! In this unit you will read magazine-style information texts about venomous creatures on land and in the sea. You will learn how writers choose their tone, how to tell facts from opinions, and how to write a gripping article about a dangerous animal.
objectives: Explain the purpose and tone of information texts, and how tone can be serious or light-hearted.
Tell the difference between facts and opinions in articles.
Use adverbs and adverbial phrases of time, frequency, place and manner.
Use modal verbs to show how possible something is.
Work out the meaning of homonyms from context, and spot silent vowels in words.
Choose words with the right shade of meaning, and write an article about a dangerous animal.

texts.title: The Venom Club – Venomous Land Creatures
texts.summary: This lively article is about venomous snakes. It explains that snakes are cold-blooded and get their warmth from their surroundings, and it describes their ‘super skills’ under fun subheadings such as Strong Scales, Stealth and Super Senses. There are about 3,500 known species of snake, but only a small number can seriously harm people.

texts.title: The Venom Club – Venomous Sea Creatures
texts.summary: This part of the article dives into the ocean to meet the box jellyfish, which has a body shape unlike other jellyfish, and the cone snail, a highly skilled hunter. The writer argues that, although these creatures are dangerous, they are also valuable and need to be protected.

vocab.meaning: Able to inject a poison (venom) by biting or stinging.
vocab.example: A cone snail is venomous.

vocab.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
vocab.example: The snake is the predator and the frog is its prey.

vocab.meaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
vocab.example: Mice are prey for many snakes.

vocab.meaning: Having a body temperature that changes with the temperature around it.
vocab.example: Snakes are cold-blooded, so they bask in the sun.

vocab.meaning: The feeling or attitude that a piece of writing shows, for example serious or light-hearted.
vocab.example: The article has a fun, light-hearted tone.

vocab.meaning: Something that can be checked and proved to be true.
vocab.example: Box jellyfish live in the ocean.

vocab.meaning: What someone thinks or believes. It cannot be proved.
vocab.example: I think box jellyfish are amazing.

vocab.meaning: A word that is spelt and said the same as another word but has a different meaning.
vocab.example: ‘Scales’ can be the plates on a snake’s skin or a machine for weighing.

vocab.meaning: To protect something so that it is not damaged or lost.
vocab.example: We must conserve ocean creatures.

vocab.meaning: To hide and then attack suddenly.
vocab.example: Many snakes ambush their prey.

cards.front: What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?

cards.front: What does ‘tone’ mean in writing?

Musical notes going up and down

units.title: What a Classic!
units.overview: Why do people still read stories that were written nearly 200 years ago? In this unit you will read extracts from Charles Dickens’s famous novel Oliver Twist. You will learn what makes a book a ‘classic’, how stories can be told from different viewpoints, and how to write direct and reported speech correctly.
objectives: Explain what makes literature a classic.
Identify first-person and third-person viewpoints in stories.
Change direct speech into reported speech, and punctuate both correctly.
Use personal and possessive pronouns correctly.
Use apostrophes for possession and for contractions.
Apply spelling rules, such as ‘i before e except after c’, and write a diary entry from a character’s viewpoint.

texts.title: Oliver Twist: The Workhouse
texts.kind: Extract from a classic novel by Charles Dickens
texts.summary: Oliver is an orphan who lives in a workhouse, where the boys are given only a small bowl of thin porridge called gruel. The hungry boys decide that someone must ask for more, and Oliver is chosen. When he walks up to the master and asks for more, the adults are shocked, and Oliver is treated as if he has committed a crime.

texts.title: Oliver Twist: The Artful Dodger
texts.kind: Extract from a classic novel by Charles Dickens
texts.summary: After a week of walking, a tired and hungry Oliver reaches a small town on the way to London. There he meets a confident boy called the Artful Dodger, who buys him food and offers to take him to a man in London who will give him somewhere to sleep.

texts.title: Oliver Twist: Oliver Got Caught!
texts.kind: Extract from a classic novel by Charles Dickens
texts.summary: Oliver watches in horror as the Dodger steals a gentleman’s handkerchief at a bookstall. Confused and frightened, Oliver runs away, so the crowd chases him, shouting ‘Stop, thief!’ Oliver is blamed for a crime that he did not commit.

vocab.meaning: A book that has been admired for a long time because it is very well written and its ideas still matter today.
vocab.example: Oliver Twist is a classic novel.

vocab.meaning: In the past, a place where very poor people lived and had to work in return for food and a bed.
vocab.example: Oliver grew up in a workhouse.

vocab.meaning: A thin, watery porridge.
vocab.example: The boys ate one small bowl of gruel.

vocab.meaning: The position from which a story is told. In the first person, the narrator says ‘I’. In the third person, the narrator says ‘he’, ‘she’ or ‘they’.
vocab.example: Oliver Twist is told in the third person.

vocab.meaning: The exact words that someone says, written inside inverted commas.
vocab.example: “I want some more,” said Oliver.

vocab.meaning: Telling what someone said without using their exact words.
vocab.example: Oliver said that he wanted some more.

vocab.meaning: A word that shows who owns something, such as ‘mine’, ‘yours’, ‘his’, ‘hers’, ‘ours’ and ‘theirs’.
vocab.example: That bowl is mine.

vocab.meaning: A punctuation mark (’) that shows possession (Oliver’s bowl) or missing letters (didn’t).
vocab.example: The boy’s feet were sore.

vocab.meaning: Two words shortened into one, with an apostrophe where the letters are missing.
vocab.example: ‘Do not’ becomes ‘don’t’.

vocab.meaning: A personal piece of writing about what happened on a particular day and how the writer felt.
vocab.example: Oliver wrote a diary entry about the day he was blamed.

sb.title: Getting Started and Let’s Learn: What makes literature a classic?
sb.tip: Classics were written long ago, are very well written and have ideas that still matter to readers today.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: Oliver Twist – The Artful Dodger
sb.tip: What clues tell you how far Oliver has walked and how he feels?

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Personal and possessive pronouns
sb.tip: Personal pronouns replace names (he, they). Possessive pronouns show ownership (mine, ours).

sb.title: Reading Part 2: Oliver Twist – Oliver Got Caught! and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: Why does Oliver run, and why does the crowd think he is the thief?

sb.title: Language Focus – Punctuation: Apostrophes
sb.tip: For one owner, add ’s (the boy’s). For plural owners ending in s, add just the apostrophe (the boys’).

sb.title: Speaking: Acting out a scene
sb.tip: Use your voice, face and body to show how your character feels.

sb.title: Writing: A diary entry to express a viewpoint
sb.tip: Write as Oliver in the first person. Include the date, what happened and how you felt.

sb.title: Unit Self-reflection
sb.tip: Would you like to read the whole of Oliver Twist one day? Why?

cards.front: What makes a book a classic?
cards.back: It was written some time ago, it is very well written, and its characters and ideas still matter to readers today.

cards.front: Who wrote Oliver Twist?
cards.back: Charles Dickens.

cards.front: Why does Oliver get into trouble in the workhouse?
cards.back: He asks for more food, and the people in charge are shocked.

cards.front: Change to reported speech: ‘I am hungry,’ said Oliver.
cards.back: Oliver said that he was hungry.

cards.front: ‘The boy’s bowls’ or ‘the boys’ bowls’?
cards.back: ‘The boy’s bowls’ belong to one boy. ‘The boys’ bowls’ belong to more than one boy.

cards.front: How can you tell a story is in the first person?

practice.q: Which sentence is reported speech?
options: Oliver said that he wanted some more.
practice.explain: Reported speech tells us what was said without the exact words or inverted commas.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: “Please, sir, I want some more” said Oliver.
“Please, sir, I want some more,” said Oliver.
“Please, sir, I want some more”, said Oliver.
Please, sir, I want some more, said Oliver.
practice.explain: The comma goes inside the inverted commas, before ‘said’.

practice.q: Which word follows the rule ‘i before e except after c’?

practice.q: Which is a possessive pronoun?

practice.explain: ‘Its’ shows possession and never has an apostrophe. ‘It’s’ means ‘it is’.

practice.explain: The narrator uses ‘I’ and ‘my’, so it is the first person.

practice.q: What is the contraction of ‘they have’?

units.title: What an Act!
units.overview: Lights, curtain, action! In this unit you will read play scripts: a short play based on Oliver Twist and a play based on a Native American folktale. You will learn how play scripts are different from stories, how writers use stage directions and dramatic conventions, and how to write and perform a one-act play of your own.
objectives: Compare play scripts with narratives.
Identify dramatic conventions, such as dialogue, a narrator, asides, costumes, scenery, props, lighting and sound effects.
Use relative pronouns and relative clauses (‘who’, ‘whom’, ‘whose’, ‘which’ and ‘that’).
Use roots, prefixes and suffixes to work out word meanings.
Spell words with stressed and unstressed vowel sounds.
Use figurative language and modal verbs, and write a play script with dialogue and stage directions.

texts.title: Oliver Twist
texts.kind: Play script based on the classic novel
texts.summary: The workhouse scene from Oliver Twist is turned into a short play. A narrator sets the scene, stage directions tell the actors what to do, and the hungry boys push Oliver to ask for more. When he does, Mr Bumble and Mr Limbkins are outraged.

texts.title: Mooin: The Bear’s Child
texts.kind: Play script (adapted from a Native American folktale)
texts.summary: Sigo’s cruel stepfather takes him hunting against his mother’s wishes, then tricks him into a cave and traps him there. Glooscap, the Great Chief, punishes the stepfather and calls the forest animals to help. Only Mooinsk, the mother bear, is strong enough to move the rock. Sigo lives with the bears and learns the forest’s secrets. In the end he returns to his human mother and takes the name Mooin.

vocab.meaning: The written text of a play, with the characters’ lines and stage directions.
vocab.example: We read the play script aloud in groups.

vocab.meaning: Instructions in a play script, usually in brackets, that tell actors how to move or speak, or describe lighting and sound.
vocab.example: (Oliver walks slowly to the master.)

vocab.meaning: The words that the characters speak to each other.
vocab.example: The dialogue is short and lively.

vocab.meaning: A person who tells the audience what is happening.
vocab.example: The narrator introduces the setting.

vocab.meaning: Words a character says to the audience that the other characters on stage do not hear.
vocab.example: The stepfather tells the audience his plan in an aside.

vocab.meaning: Objects that actors use on stage.
vocab.example: The bowls and spoons are props.

vocab.meaning: The painted background and objects that show where a scene takes place.
vocab.example: The scenery showed a dark forest.

vocab.meaning: At the side of the stage, where the audience cannot see.
vocab.example: A loud noise came from offstage.

vocab.meaning: A word such as ‘who’, ‘whom’, ‘whose’, ‘which’ or ‘that’ that starts a clause giving more information.
vocab.example: The actor who played Oliver was excellent.

vocab.meaning: One of the main parts that a play is divided into. Each act can contain several scenes.
vocab.example: There is a break at the end of Act 1.

sb.title: Be Curious and Getting Started
sb.tip: Talk about theatres and what actors do to prepare for a play.

sb.title: Let’s Learn: Play scripts vs narratives
sb.tip: Play scripts have stage directions, acts and scenes, and a list of characters. Narratives have chapters and description.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: Oliver Twist (play script)
sb.tip: Read the stage directions carefully. They tell you how the characters feel and move.

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Relative pronouns and relative clauses

sb.title: Language Focus – Vocabulary: Roots, suffixes and prefixes
sb.tip: Roots carry meaning. ‘Tele’ means far, ‘graph’ means writing or drawing, and ‘bio’ means life.

sb.title: Word Structure: Stressed and unstressed vowel sounds
sb.tip: Unstressed vowels often sound like ‘uh’, as in ‘hist(o)ry’. Say the word in an exaggerated way to help you spell it.

sb.title: Writing: Dialogue and stage directions
sb.tip: Write the character’s name, then their words. Put stage directions in brackets.

sb.title: Getting Started and Let’s Learn: Dramatic conventions in play scripts
sb.tip: Dramatic conventions, such as asides, lighting and sound effects, help to make a play believable and exciting.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: Mooin: The Bear’s Child
sb.tip: Look for the aside. Who is the character speaking to?

sb.title: Language Focus – Vocabulary: Figurative language
sb.tip: Find similes, metaphors and personification in sentences about the play.

sb.title: Reading Part 2: Mooin: The Bear’s Child and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: How do the offstage noises and lighting build tension?

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: More about modal verbs
sb.tip: Modal verbs can be used to make polite requests, for example ‘Could I…?’ and ‘May I…?’

sb.title: Speaking: Presenting a play
sb.tip: Learn your lines, face the audience, project your voice and stay in character.

sb.title: Writing: Play script for a one-act play
sb.tip: Plan the characters, setting and plot. Then write the dialogue and helpful stage directions.

sb.title: Unit Self-reflection
sb.tip: Did you prefer reading or performing plays? Why?

cards.front: Name three features of a play script.
cards.back: For example, a list of characters, dialogue, stage directions in brackets, and acts and scenes.

cards.front: What is an aside?
cards.back: Words a character says to the audience that the other characters on stage cannot hear.

cards.front: What are props?
cards.back: Objects that actors use on stage, such as bowls, spoons or a lantern.

cards.front: When do you use ‘whose’?
cards.back: To show ownership, for example ‘The boy whose bowl it was licked it clean.’

cards.front: Who frees Sigo from the cave?
cards.back: Mooinsk, the mother bear, moves the heavy rock.

cards.front: What does the root ‘tele’ mean?
cards.back: Far, as in ‘telephone’, ‘telescope’ and ‘television’.

practice.q: In a play script, stage directions are usually written…
options: at the end of the play
practice.explain: Stage directions usually go in brackets so that they are not read aloud as dialogue.

practice.q: Which relative pronoun completes the sentence? ‘The actor ___ played Oliver was brilliant.’
practice.explain: We use ‘who’ for people.

practice.q: What is an aside?
options: A secret comment to the audience
practice.explain: In an aside, a character speaks to the audience and the other characters do not hear it.

practice.q: Which word contains the root ‘graph’ (writing or drawing)?
practice.explain: An autograph is a person’s own signature, so it is a kind of writing.

practice.q: ‘The cave swallowed the light.’ What is this?
practice.explain: The cave is given a human action (swallowing), so it is personification.

practice.q: Which sentence is a polite request?
options: Could I borrow your script, please?
practice.explain: ‘Could I…?’ is a polite way to ask.

practice.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of a play script?
practice.explain: Chapters belong to narratives such as novels, not play scripts.

practice.q: ‘Offstage’ means…
options: in the middle of the stage
at the side of the stage where the audience cannot see
practice.explain: Offstage is out of the audience’s sight.

units.title: At the Movies
units.overview: How does a story in a book become a film? In this unit you will read an extract from The Jungle Book and then see a scene from the same story written as a film script. You will learn the language of film-making, retell a story from a different viewpoint and write a film script for a brand-new scene.
objectives: Compare novels and films, and how each one tells a story.
Identify the features of a film script, such as shots, camera directions and sound.
Use abstract nouns, and join sentences with coordinating and subordinating connectives.
Use the present perfect and past perfect verb forms.
Spell adjectives ending in ‘-able’ and ‘-ible’.
Choose powerful words and phrases, and write a film script for a new scene.

texts.title: Mowgli’s Brothers
texts.kind: Extract from The Jungle Book by Rudyard Kipling
texts.summary: Father Wolf and Mother Wolf hear that Shere Khan, the tiger, is hunting near their home. A small human baby wanders into their den, and Mother Wolf protects him from Shere Khan and names him Mowgli. At the meeting of the wolf pack, Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther speak up for Mowgli, so that he can stay and grow up in the jungle.

texts.title: The Defeat of Shere Khan
texts.kind: Film script based on The Jungle Book
texts.summary: In this action-packed film scene, an older Mowgli faces Shere Khan. Baloo fights bravely to protect him, and vultures carry Mowgli away from danger. When a tree catches fire, Mowgli ties a burning branch to Shere Khan’s tail, and the frightened tiger runs off into the jungle.

vocab.meaning: The written plan of a film, with dialogue, actions and directions for the camera and sound.
vocab.example: The film script tells the camera to zoom in on Mowgli.

vocab.meaning: A series of drawings that shows each shot of a film in order.
vocab.example: We drew a storyboard before writing our script.

vocab.meaning: One continuous piece of filming from one camera position.
vocab.example: The first shot shows the tall grass at the edge of the jungle.

vocab.meaning: To make the camera image move closer to, or further away from, something.
vocab.example: The camera zooms in on the tiger’s eyes.

vocab.meaning: The music and sounds that you hear in a film.
vocab.example: The soundtrack got louder as the tiger came closer.

vocab.meaning: A noun for an idea, feeling or quality that you cannot see or touch.
vocab.example: Mother Wolf showed great courage.

vocab.meaning: A word that joins clauses or sentences, such as ‘and’, ‘but’, ‘because’ or ‘although’.
vocab.example: Mowgli was small, but he was fearless.

vocab.meaning: The name the animals give to Mowgli, because he is a human child.
vocab.example: “The man-cub is mine!” growled Shere Khan.

vocab.meaning: Behaving as if you are better or more important than other people.
vocab.example: Shere Khan was arrogant and did not ask permission to hunt.

vocab.meaning: A verb form using ‘had’ that shows one past action happened before another.
vocab.example: Mowgli had left before the tiger arrived.

sb.title: Be Curious and Getting Started
sb.tip: Talk about going to the cinema and what makes a film enjoyable.

sb.title: Let’s Learn: Novels vs films
sb.tip: A novel uses words for everything. A film can show the setting, sounds and expressions on screen.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: Mowgli’s Brothers
sb.tip: Notice how each character reacts to the ‘man-cub’. Who wants to protect him, and who wants him as prey?

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Abstract nouns
sb.tip: Many abstract nouns end in suffixes such as ‘-tion’, ‘-ment’, ‘-ance’ and ‘-ism’ (decision, amazement, importance, heroism).

sb.title: Reading Part 2: Mowgli’s Brothers and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: What do Baloo and Bagheera do to help Mowgli join the pack?

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Joining sentences
sb.tip: Coordinating connectives (and, but, so) join clauses of equal importance. Subordinating connectives (when, because, although) add a dependent clause.

sb.title: Word Structure: Suffixes -able and -ible
sb.tip: If the root is a whole word, ‘-able’ is more common (comfortable). If it is not a whole word, ‘-ible’ is more common (horrible). Check in a dictionary.

sb.title: Writing: A story retold from a different viewpoint
sb.tip: Choose a character and retell the events as that character, using ‘I’ and showing their thoughts and feelings.

sb.title: Getting Started and Let’s Learn: Features of a film script
sb.tip: Film scripts include shots, camera directions (pan and zoom), the setting, sound and dialogue.

sb.title: Reading Part 1: The Defeat of Shere Khan
sb.tip: Picture each shot as you read. What would the camera show?

sb.title: Language Focus – Grammar: Verb forms: Present perfect and past perfect
sb.tip: Present perfect uses ‘has’ or ‘have’ (has spoken). Past perfect uses ‘had’ (had spoken).

sb.title: Reading Part 2: The Defeat of Shere Khan and Reading Comprehension
sb.tip: Put the action in order. Which event is the turning point?

sb.title: Language Focus – Vocabulary: Choosing the right words and phrases
sb.tip: Replace general words with precise ones, for example ‘furious’ instead of ‘angry’ or ‘sprinted’ instead of ‘ran fast’.

sb.title: Listening: Behind the scenes

units.title: The Art of Persuasion
units.overview: How do you change someone’s mind? In this unit you will read persuasive commentaries about languages that are disappearing, a persuasive article about plastic in our oceans, and letters written to convince people to act. You will learn the tricks that persuasive writers use and write a persuasive letter of your own.
objectives: Identify the features of a persuasive commentary and a persuasive letter.
Use persuasive words and phrases to express opinions and give reasons.
Use relative pronouns and relative clauses to add information.
Choose between formal and informal register for different audiences.
Add suffixes to root words to make new words.
Use adverbs and adverbial phrases to link ideas, and write a persuasive letter.

texts.title: Disappearing Languages
texts.summary: About 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today, but around half of them could disappear. The writer explains why this happens and why it matters: languages carry special knowledge about places, nature and culture. The commentary asks questions, gives answers and suggests ways to save these languages.

texts.title: The Basque Language Revival
texts.summary: Basque is a very old language spoken in a region of Spain and France. It was once discouraged, but people kept it alive through conversation, songs and poems. Today it is taught from preschool to university, and technology and games help young people to use it. The writer calls this work a shining example.

texts.title: Danger in Our Oceans
texts.summary: Plastic is made of strong chains of molecules, so it takes a very long time to break down. Instead, it breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics, which harm sea creatures and can even end up in our food. The writer argues that we all need to take responsibility.

texts.title: Letters to Convince You
texts.kind: A persuasive email and a persuasive letter
texts.summary: Two young writers try to persuade others to cut down on single-use plastic. One writes a formal email asking for reusable cups instead of plastic ones. The other writes a chatty, informal letter to a friend, suggesting packed lunches in reusable containers instead of fast-food packaging.

vocab.meaning: To make someone agree with you or do something by giving them good reasons.
vocab.example: She persuaded the class to recycle more.

vocab.meaning: A piece of writing that gives the writer’s opinion and explanation about an issue.
vocab.example: The commentary argued that we should save small languages.

vocab.meaning: What someone thinks or believes about something.
vocab.example: In my opinion, every school should have recycling bins.

vocab.meaning: How formal or informal language is, depending on who you are talking or writing to.
vocab.example: Use a formal register in a letter to the head teacher.

vocab.meaning: The most powerful or important.
vocab.example: A dominant language can take over smaller ones.

vocab.meaning: Belonging to a place from the very beginning, before others arrived.
vocab.example: Basque is an indigenous language of the region.

vocab.meaning: Made to be used only once and then thrown away.
vocab.example: Single-use plastic cups cause pollution.

vocab.meaning: To break down naturally over time.
vocab.example: Leaves decompose, but plastic takes hundreds of years.

vocab.meaning: Tiny pieces of plastic that come from larger plastic breaking down.
vocab.example: Fish can swallow microplastics.

vocab.meaning: Scattered rubbish or broken pieces.
vocab.example: Plastic debris washed up on the beach.

cards.front: What does a persuasive commentary do?
cards.back: It highlights a problem, gives accurate information, suggests a solution and tries to convince the reader.

cards.front: Formal or informal? ‘Hi there, buddy! Want to try packed lunches with me?’
cards.back: Informal. It uses a chatty greeting and a short, friendly question.

cards.front: Why do languages disappear?
cards.back: For example, parents want children to learn a dominant language for jobs, and some societies have stopped people using their own languages.

cards.front: Why is plastic dangerous for sea creatures?
cards.back: It does not decompose naturally. It breaks into microplastics that animals swallow and that can clog their digestive systems.

cards.front: Name three persuasive phrases.
